0.1 This Indian

FOREWORD

Standard was adopted by the Indian Standards Institution on 29 October 1982, after the draft finalized by the Photographic Materials Sectional Committee had been approved by the Chemical Division Council. 0.2 In the preparation of this standard considerable assistance derived from ASA.PH-2.2-1966 `Sensitometry of Photographic issued by the American Standards Association. has been Papers'

0.3 In reporting the result of a test or analysis made in accordance with this standard, if the final value, observed or calculated, is to be rounded off, it shall be done in accordance with IS : 2-1960*.

1. SCOPE 1.1 This standard prescribes a method of determining certain sensitometric characteristics of developing-out black-and-white photographic papers intended for contact or projection printing of photographic negatives. It specifies the exposing and processing conditions to be used in determining the density-versus-log-exposure curve of the photographic papers. It also specifies procedures for deriving numerical values for such significant sensitometric characteristics as speed, maximum shoulder density, density range, and log exposure range.
2. EXPOSING AND PROCESSING

2.1 Conditioning the Sample Before Testing - The test sample <hall be in equilibrium wlith an atmosphere maintained at a temperature of 20 & 5�C and a relative humidity of 55 f 10 percent.

2.2.3 Modulation -- The spectral transmission density of the light modulator ( that is grey scale ) shall not differ by more than 0.06 for any two lvavelengths within the wavelength range of 350 to 700 millimicrons. 2.2.3.1 For continuous modulation of the exposure along the sensitometric test strip, the exposure ratio shall not be greater than 2 per cm If stepped increments are used, and shall be uniform along the strip. the minimum exposure increment shall be a factor of the square root of 2 per step, and each step shall have a minimum width of 0.8 cm. 2.2.4 Quality of Radiant Energy Incident on the Sample - The spectral energy dystribution of the modulated radiant energy on the sample shall be equal to that of a blackbody radiator at a temperature of 3 000 f 25�K. This distribution may be very closely approximated by means of a tungsten-filament lamp operated at a colour temperature of 3 000 * 25�K or, in the interest of longer lamp life, by means of a tungstenfilament lamp operated at a colour temperature of 2 850�K in combination with a suitable filter for converting the spectral energy distribution approximately to that of a blackbody radiator at 3 000 k 25'K. 2.2.5 Tolerance of Exposure - The product of illuminance and time ( 1.t = exposure ) shall be expressed in absolute photometric units and shall be maintained within & 5 percent of the intended values, or approximately If 0.02 log units. 2.3 Processing the Sample - The test sample shall be processed as soon as possib;e after exposure to avoid possible change of latent image. The time lapse between exposure and development shall not exceed 2 hours, and the exposed sample shall be stored at a temperature of 20 f: 5�C and a relative humidity of 55 & 10 percent. 2.3.1 Developing Solution 50�C ) ) 500 3.1 ml g

2.3.2 One part of solution shall be freshly diluted with 2 parts of distilled water and used at a temperature of 20 f 0.5"C for developing each test. 2.3.3 Developing Technique - Development shall be carried out in a horizontal 300 mm x 350 mm tray containing 2 litres of developer. During development the sensitometrically exposed samples shall be held in a plane close and parallel to the bottom of the tray by means of any device that shall not interfere physically or chemically with the exposed area Five of to such an extent as to influence the final sensitometric result. the 35 mm x 250 mm senGtometric strips fastened to a 200 mm x 250 mm glass plate may be conveniently handled in this manner. 2.3.4 The developer shall be agitated during development to an extent equivalent to that provided by rocking the tray at a rate of 74 complete A cycle shall be one motion in each of the four cycles per minute. Such agitation or rocking of the tray may be facilitated by directions. using a block 65 mm x 50 mm x 20 mm under the tray centre with the block side' parallel to the tray sides. 2.3.5 Other techniques to between the purchaser of development and the supplier. may be employed as agreed

2.3.9 Washing -- The samples shall be washed in running water at a temperature of 20 & 5�C for 15 minutes or washed in six changes of These conditions of washwater with 5 minutes between each change. ing may be used for sensitometric purposes only and may not imply permanence of the print. 2.3.10 Drying - All samples shall be air-dried in an atmosphere maintained within the limits of 25 h 10�C and a relative humidity of 55 f 10 percent. 3. CONSTRUCTING

THE D LOG E CURVE

3.1 Plotting the Curve - The optical density of the sensitometric steps shall be measured using a suitable reflectance densitometer. The reflection densities (Dr) as ordinates shall be plotted against their corresponding log exposure ( log E ) values as abscissas, and a smooth curve shall be drawn through the plotted points, E shall be expressed in metrecandle-seconds ( see Fig. 1 ). The scale units on the graph paper for the abscissa and the ordinate shall have equal spacing. For brevity, the reflection density will be referred to as density and the symbol D used without the subscript r in this standard.

The specified sensitomctric characteristics shall be drived from the coordinates of two points, a and b, found on the D log E curve ( Fig. 1 ) in the high-light and shadow regions, respectively. The point a is localed on the toe of the D log E curve where the density is 0'!5 above the sum of the base density and the fog density ( see 4.5 ). The point b is locaterl on the shoulder of the curve at 0.9 of the maximum shoulder density, DC ( see 4.4 ).

4.2 Log Exposure values for the limiting
Log Exposure

Range -- The difference between the points b and a shall be called log exposure = log Et, log Ea

Range

4.3 Density Range - The difference between the ordinate values, expressed as in 4.2, for the limiting points b and a shall be called density range. Density Range = Db Da

4.4 Maximum Shoulder Density - The ordinate value for the point c shall be called maximum shoulder density and shall be designated as DC. Point c is the point on the shoulder of the curve where the gradient has diminished to 0.05. Usually, the greatest density reached by the curve approximates this value. 4.5 Fog Density - Fog density shall be the reflection density difference between an unexposed, processed test sample, which qives the sum ,of the base density and the fog density, and an unexposed, fixed-out 7
